chapterNote: A brief coda. The empire rolls on, taxing land and sea, but the last word is Mordecai: a captive's descendant risen to be second in the kingdom, using his power not for himself but for the good and the peace of his people. The book that never names God ends on a portrait of exactly what His hidden providence had been building toward — a faithful man positioned to bless the many.

1.text: Now King Ahasuerus imposed a tribute over the land and the coastlands of the sea.

2.text: And all his acts of power and might, and the full account of the greatness to which the king raised Mordecai, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?
2.notes: The chronicles return one last time. The same royal annals that once recorded Mordecai's forgotten good deed (2:23; 6:1–2) now record his greatness — the record that heaven used to lift him is where his story is finally kept.

3.text: For Mordecai the Jew was second only to King Ahasuerus. He was great among the Jews and beloved by the multitude of his people, for he sought the good of his people and spoke peace to all his kindred.
3.amp: he sought the welfare [tov — the good] of his people and spoke peace [shalom] to all his descendants.
3.notes: The book closes on a diaspora Jew who used the highest place in a pagan empire to 'seek the good of his people and speak peace' — the very calling Jeremiah gave the exiles: seek the welfare of the city where you are sent (Jer. 29:7). Providence had spent nine chapters positioning him for this: power held for the blessing of others.
